title: CONTEXT MATTERS: HOW FALSE TEACHERS MAKE THE BIBLE SAY WHAT IT NEVER SAID
paragraphs:
CONTEXT MATTERS: HOW FALSE TEACHERS MAKE THE BIBLE SAY WHAT IT NEVER SAID
The most dangerous lie in church may not sound like a lie at all. It may sound biblical—because someone attached a Bible verse to it.
There is something more dangerous than a person standing in front of you saying, “I reject the Bible.”
It is someone opening the Bible…
reading from it…
quoting it confidently…
and then making God say something God never said.
That is what makes deception frightening.
Sometimes deception does not arrive carrying a sign that says FALSE TEACHER.
Sometimes it carries a Bible.
Sometimes it knows Greek words.
Sometimes it has millions of views.
Sometimes it cries while preaching.
Sometimes it says exactly what wounded people desperately want to hear.
And sometimes the verse being quoted is completely real.
The deception is hiding in what happened to the verse after it was removed from its context.
Please understand this before reading another sentence:
A Bible verse can be quoted accurately and still be used dishonestly.
The words may belong to Scripture while the meaning being attached to them does not.
And perhaps one of the most disturbing examples of this happens before Jesus ever begins His public ministry.
Jesus is in the wilderness.
Hungry.
Physically weakened after fasting.
And Satan comes to tempt Him.
But notice something unsettling about the temptation recorded in Matthew 4.
The devil does not merely tempt Jesus with obviously evil words.
At one point…
he quotes Scripture.
Matthew tells us that the devil takes Jesus to the holy city, places Him on the pinnacle of the temple, and challenges Him to throw Himself down.
Then comes the chilling part:
“For it is written…”
Those words should make every Christian pay attention.
Because what follows really is written.
The devil draws from Psalm 91, appealing to God's promise concerning His angels and their protection.
He has Scripture in his mouth…
while rebellion is in his purpose.
Jesus answers Scripture with Scripture, refusing to put God to the test.
Think about what just happened.
The issue was not whether Satan could locate words in the Bible.
He could.
The issue was whether he was submitting to what God actually meant.
He wasn't.
And that should permanently destroy one dangerous assumption:
Someone quoting Scripture is not automatically someone teaching Scripture faithfully.
The serpent's strategy is ancient.
In Genesis 3, the attack begins around God's words:
“Did God actually say…?”
By Matthew 4, the strategy has become even more sophisticated.
Now Scripture itself is being weaponized against the Son of God.
The enemy does not always need to convince people to throw away their Bibles.
Sometimes he only needs to teach them how to misuse them.
And that is why context matters.
Not because context is an academic luxury for theologians.
Not because ordinary Christians need to become experts in ancient languages before they can understand anything.
Context matters because meaning matters.
And when meaning is corrupted, God's Word can be made to appear to endorse things God's Word never endorsed.
You have probably seen it happen.
Someone says:
“Judge not.”
Conversation over.

Except Jesus' words in Matthew 7 were not a universal prohibition against recognizing sin, discerning falsehood, or making moral judgments. Jesus condemns hypocritical judgment and commands the person judging to deal with the log in his own eye so that he can see clearly to address the speck in his brother's eye. Later in the same chapter, Jesus warns about false prophets and says they will be recognized by their fruits.
You cannot obey that warning without discernment.
Someone says:
“I can do all things through Christ.”
Therefore…
I will win.
I will become wealthy.
I will get the promotion.
My business cannot fail.
Every dream I have must succeed because Philippians 4:13 guarantees it.
Except Paul was not writing Philippians from a luxury resort explaining the secret of unlimited personal achievement.
He was describing contentment.
He knew abundance.
He knew need.
He knew hunger.
He knew plenty.
He knew deprivation.
And in those changing circumstances, Christ strengthened him to endure faithfully.
That makes Philippians 4:13 more beautiful, not less.
The verse is not primarily saying, “Jesus will make every ambition succeed.”
It is teaching something stronger:
Christ is sufficient even when circumstances are not.
Then there is Jeremiah 29:11.
“For I know the plans I have for you…”
Beautiful words.
True words.

But they were spoken within God's message to exiles in Babylon. Jeremiah had just told them that their exile would not disappear tomorrow. They were to build houses, plant gardens, establish families, seek the welfare of the city—and after the appointed period, God would fulfill His promise.
The promise was not originally a personalized guarantee that every modern believer's immediate plans will prosper.
The original audience was staring at decades of exile.
Context does not destroy hope.
Context deepens it.
Because biblical hope is not:
Nothing painful will happen to me.
Biblical hope is:
God remains faithful even when obedience takes me through circumstances I never wanted.
That difference matters.
Because somewhere tonight a Christian is wondering why God “broke His promise.”
Maybe God never broke it.
Maybe someone taught that believer a promise God never made.
And that can leave terrible wounds.
A mother prays for her child and someone tells her that sufficient faith guarantees the outcome she desperately wants.
The outcome does not come.
Now she does not merely carry grief.
She carries guilt.
“Maybe I didn't believe enough.”

A struggling family sends money they cannot comfortably afford because someone isolated a passage and persuaded them that giving to a particular ministry would unlock guaranteed financial multiplication.
Nothing changes.
They quietly wonder whether God failed.
A sick believer hears a preacher imply that physical healing is guaranteed immediately if faith is strong enough.
The sickness remains.
Now the person fights disease…
and shame.
A lonely Christian is told that a particular verse guarantees marriage.
Years pass.
Confusion becomes resentment.
Someone pursuing a dream is told that God promised success.
The door closes.
Now disappointment becomes a crisis of faith.
And beneath all these wounds is sometimes the same devastating possibility:
They are angry with God for failing to keep something God never promised them.
This is why false teaching is not harmless.
Bad theology eventually bleeds.
It reaches marriages.
Bank accounts.
Hospital rooms.
Funerals.
Consciences.
Families.
Churches.
And souls.
Peter knew Scripture could be distorted.
In 2 Peter 3:16 he speaks about people mishandling difficult portions of Paul's letters and says they “distort” them, as they do the other Scriptures.
The Greek verb is striking:
στρεβλοῦσιν — streblousin
It comes from στρεβλόω — strebloō, meaning to twist or distort.
The picture is not merely misunderstanding something accidentally.
It carries the idea of wrenching something away from its proper shape.
Peter's warning is sobering: Scripture can be twisted.
The Bible itself therefore warns you about people who misuse the Bible.
Read that again.
The Bible warns you about people who use the Bible wrongly.
Which means saying, “But they quoted Scripture,” is not enough.
The question must become:
Did they handle Scripture faithfully?
Paul gives Timothy a powerful standard.
The Greek text of 2 Timothy 2:15 reads:
σπούδασον σεαυτὸν δόκιμον παραστῆσαι τῷ θεῷ, ἐργάτην ἀνεπαίσχυντον, ὀρθοτομοῦντα τὸν λόγον τῆς ἀληθείας.
Spoudason seauton dokimon parastēsai tō Theō, ergatēn anepaischynton, orthotomounta ton logon tēs alētheias.
The heart of Paul's command is powerful: be diligent to present yourself approved before God, a worker without cause for shame, ὀρθοτομοῦντα — orthotomounta the word of truth.

The term is commonly rendered “rightly handling” or “accurately handling,” and its imagery has been discussed in terms of making a straight cut or maintaining a straight course. Whatever precise metaphor Paul intended, the practical force is clear: God's truth is not ours to bend into whatever shape serves our agenda.
There is a straightness to faithful interpretation.
And there is a twisting to deception.
But here is where this article becomes uncomfortable.
Because false teachers are not the only people capable of taking Scripture out of context.
We do it too.
Maybe not from a pulpit.
Maybe not intentionally.
Maybe nobody knows.
But we can open Scripture looking less for God's meaning than for God's permission.
We already want the relationship…
so we search for a verse that will bless it.
We already want revenge…
so we find biblical language that makes our bitterness sound righteous.
We already love money…
so we collect prosperity verses while ignoring warnings about greed.
We already want to avoid forgiving someone…
so we construct theology around our wound.
We already want a political ideology to be unquestionably righteous…
so we recruit Jesus as its mascot.
We already have an opinion…
then open the Bible looking for ammunition.
And suddenly Scripture is no longer functioning as the sword that cuts us.
We are using it as a weapon to cut everybody else.
That is where context becomes more than interpretation.
It becomes surrender.
Because faithful Bible reading requires something painful:
allowing God to disagree with you.
You do not stand above Scripture as its judge.
Scripture stands above you.
You do not approach the Bible saying:
“Confirm me.”
You approach saying:
“Correct me.”
Not:
“Give me something I can post.”
But:
“Lord, show me what You actually said.”
Not:
“Help me win this argument.”
But:
“Help me obey You even if Your Word destroys my argument.”
That is discipleship.
And it requires humility.
When reading a verse, slow down.
Read what comes before it.
Read what comes after it.
Ask who is speaking.
Ask who is being addressed.
Ask what problem is being confronted.
Ask what kind of biblical writing you are reading—narrative, poetry, wisdom, prophecy, Gospel, letter, apocalyptic literature.
Ask whether something is being described or commanded.
Ask how the passage fits within the chapter, book, and ultimately the whole testimony of Scripture.
And above everything else…
look toward Christ.
Because Christianity is not ultimately about collecting inspirational sentences.
Scripture leads us into God's redemptive story centered in Jesus Christ.
Jesus Himself confronted people who possessed biblical knowledge while missing the One to whom Scripture pointed.

In John 5:39–40 He tells His opponents that they search the Scriptures because they think that in them they possess eternal life, yet those Scriptures testify about Him—and they refuse to come to Him for life.
Imagine knowing verses…
and missing Jesus.
Imagine defending theology…
and refusing the Savior.
Imagine winning arguments about Scripture…
while resisting the Lord of Scripture.
That is terrifying.
Because correct interpretation is not merely about becoming intellectually superior to false teachers.
The destination is not pride.
It is Christ.
Truth should lead toward worship.
Truth should lead toward repentance.
Truth should expose sin.
Truth should magnify grace.
Truth should humble us before the cross.
And at the cross, something astonishing happens.
Every self-righteous person discovers he needs mercy.
Every sinner discovers sin is more serious than he imagined.
Every broken person discovers grace is more magnificent than she dared hope.
The Gospel does not say you are basically good and Jesus came to improve you.
It says sin has separated humanity from holy God, and we cannot rescue ourselves.
Jesus Christ, the sinless Son of God, came into the world.
He lived the righteousness we failed to live.
He died for sinners.
He bore judgment.
He was buried.
He rose again.
And now forgiveness and reconciliation with God are offered through Him.
Repent.
Believe the Gospel.
Come to Christ.
Not the motivational Jesus created by social media.
Not the political Jesus recreated in our own image.
Not the prosperity Jesus who exists to finance our desires.
Not the permissive Jesus who never confronts sin.
Not the angry caricature who possesses truth but apparently no mercy.
Jesus Christ as Scripture reveals Him.
Full of grace and truth.
Holy.
Compassionate.
Crucified.
Risen.
Lord.
King.
Savior.
Maybe that is the scandal underneath everything.
We keep trying to rewrite Jesus…
while Jesus came to rewrite us.
We want a Christ who validates every desire.
Instead we meet a Savior who says, “Follow Me.”
We want Christianity without repentance.
He calls sinners to turn.
We want grace without lordship.
He calls us to die to ourselves.
We want truth without love or love without truth.
In Christ we encounter both grace and truth.
And perhaps you have been wounded by distorted Scripture.
Maybe somebody controlled you with Bible verses.
Maybe someone used God's Word to manipulate your money.
Maybe Scripture was quoted to silence legitimate questions.
Maybe someone made you believe every tragedy in your life happened because your faith was inadequate.
Maybe a religious leader used biblical language while living a hidden life completely contrary to what he preached.
Hear this carefully:
The abuse of Scripture does not invalidate Scripture.
The counterfeit does not make the authentic worthless.
The existence of false teachers does not make Jesus false.
Do not abandon Christ because someone misrepresented Him.
Return to Him.
Open the Gospels again.
Read slowly.
Read whole passages.
Pray.
Compare Scripture with Scripture.
Seek mature, accountable believers and faithful teachers who are willing to let the text correct them too.
Be like the Bereans in Acts 17, who received Paul's message eagerly while examining the Scriptures to see whether what they were hearing was true.
Notice the balance.
They were not cynical.
They were not gullible.
They were receptive…
and discerning.
That is spiritual maturity.
You do not have to believe every preacher because he owns a Bible.
You do not have to accept every viral Christian video because the speaker says, “God told me.”
You do not have to surrender discernment because somebody has a title.
Test what you hear.
And please…
test this article too.
Do not believe something merely because Gospel Warrior published it.
Open your Bible.
Read the passages.
Check the context.
If anything we teach contradicts Scripture, Scripture wins.
Every time.
No ministry deserves the authority that belongs to God's Word.
No preacher.
No denomination.
No influencer.
No author.
No tradition.
No Gospel Warrior.
Jesus is Lord.
That is exactly why ministries committed to biblical truth need believers who will not merely consume content but help truth travel.
Not because sharing a Facebook article earns favor with God.
It doesn't.
It cannot.
Grace cannot be bought.
Salvation cannot be purchased.
But if this message helped you recognize how easily Scripture can be distorted, you can turn that gratitude into mission.
Not to make us famous.
Someone may be blaming God for a promise He never made.
Someone may be sending money under manipulation.
Someone may be trapped beneath condemnation created by bad theology.
Someone may be slowly walking away from Christianity when what they actually need is to discover that the Jesus they rejected was a caricature somebody created.
And if this exposed something in you, do not hide behind silence.
There is no shame in admitting you are rebuilding.
Because eventually you will encounter another verse online that sounds convincing.
Return here.
Remember the wilderness.
Remember that even the devil could say:
“It is written.”
The question was what God meant.
But never confuse supporting a ministry with supporting the Gospel itself.
The Gospel does not need to be purchased.
Christ already paid the price sinners could never pay.
Share because someone needs the truth.
Give because you choose generosity.
Stay because you want to grow.
But worship Jesus Christ alone.
Not every sentence containing a Bible verse contains biblical truth.
Not every preacher holding Scripture is submitting to Scripture.
Not every message that makes you feel powerful came from God.
Sometimes the truth will comfort you.
Sometimes it will confront you.
Sometimes it will expose the belief you desperately wanted to keep.
Sometimes it will tear down the god you created in your imagination so that you can finally meet the God who actually revealed Himself.
But when Scripture is allowed to speak in context…
when Christ remains at the center…
when repentance replaces self-justification…
when grace meets the sinner who finally stops pretending…
something extraordinary happens.
The Word no longer becomes clay in our hands.
We become clay in God's.
And maybe that is what somebody reading this has needed all along.
Not another verse twisted to promise an easier life.
Not another preacher telling you exactly what you wanted to hear.
Not another Christian slogan.
But the living Christ calling you out of deception…
out of performance…
out of manipulation…
out of sin…
and into truth.
Come back to the text.
Come back to the Gospel.
Come back to Jesus.
Because the most frightening misuse of Scripture is making the Bible sound like us.
And the most beautiful moment is when we finally become quiet enough to hear what God actually said.
Never force Scripture to fit the story you want—bring your broken story to Jesus, and let His truth rewrite you.
